New encryption should not require replacing the network that carries your conversations.

Our existing hybrid envelope uses one version byte and one suite byte. In the audit fixture, a 280-byte chat becomes a 5295-byte hybrid gift wrap, compared with 2567 bytes classically. The selector is small. The cryptography carries the cost.

Relays can transport that encrypted content without implementing the inner encryption method. They still validate the outer event, enforce size and access rules, and apply any public-proof policy they support.

We have published an illustrated guide to adding encryption suites, declaring relay capabilities and handling incompatible peers without silently weakening encryption.

The new relay policies and public hybrid authentication are proposals, not released relay features. Key rotation and event references still need more work.

Crypto-agility is about being able to evolve, not choosing one encryption method forever.

PQC is one reason to upgrade today. New algorithms, new threats and different user needs will require more choices in the future.

Each client should choose the encryption suites it trusts to protect its users and their data. Each relay should define the data it accepts, the formats it can support and the validation it can actually perform. Users can then communicate through compatible relays without requiring the whole network to upgrade at once.

That is what we are proposing: explicit capabilities, compact suite identifiers and a path for adding new methods without redefining existing ones. Relays can carry opaque encrypted payloads while enforcing their declared admission rules; the endpoints choose and understand the encryption inside.

Our new guide explains the rollout with examples and diagrams. The relay and authentication extensions remain proposals for review.
